reasoning: b- present byiTla3 with emphatic ط, and the article assimilates to the sun letter ص. bukra is the Palestinian word for tomorrow.
First person b- present with ba-, long uu, and the masculine object -ak. Everyday sign-off, often bashuufak ba3deen.
Shadda doubles ظ, written TH, and the initial mu- reduces to a cluster. Taa marbuta after ف is e.
Two short i vowels in the Palestinian past shape, not sakata. Means both falling silent and keeping quiet about something.
Active participle with a long aa; ع is 3. Used for an ongoing state, saami3ni can I hear you, and also for having heard something.
Long aa in the middle, taa marbuta after م is e. A high-frequency word in Palestinian political and personal talk.
One syllable with a final cluster, ح as 7. The same noun also covers detention or seizure, but booking is the everyday sense.
Shadda doubles the خ, so khkh, and ق in wi'if is a glottal stop with two short i vowels. Said when you cannot take in any more.

reasoning: Long aa then long uu, and taa marbuta after ر is a. A faatuura is what you are asked to pay; the slip proving you paid is a waSl.
European loan with long aa and long oo. Used unchanged in Ramallah speech and media.
From French bicyclette, stressed on a long ee at the end. The everyday word, well ahead of darraaja.
Form X verbal noun; the word-initial hamza seat is not romanized. Everyday political vocabulary in Ramallah, not only written Arabic.
Literally my age is ... years, with no verb. The singular sane follows numbers from eleven up, while three to ten take sniin, so the slot decides the form.
Long ee at the start, with the hamza seat unwritten in the romanization. The ordinary Ramallah word for when, not mata.
From ma 3aleeh shi, so a long ee before the final sh, though it is often clipped shorter in fast speech. Works as both never mind and a light apology.
An everyday word, so ق glottalises, and ض is emphatic D. In formal or religious contexts such as il-qaaDi ish-shar3i you also hear q.
English loan taken in with a long ii then a long oo. Standard for the TV handset; some say rimoot with a shorter first vowel.
Long ee, not ii. The Palestinian question word for where, against MSA ayna.
Both ث become t in Palestinian, so the word is respelled تلاتة. This is the standalone counting form; before a noun it is tlaat.
The article assimilates to the sun letter س, and taa marbuta after م is e. Said by the one staying to the one going.
ث is t in Palestinian, so ثبّت is respelled تبّت with a shadda on the ب. Covers fixing or mounting something as well as confirming a booking.
Accurate as MSA, but nobody in Ramallah describes a table or a face as mustadiir in conversation. The spoken word is mdawwar.
inno with a doubled n and final o is the Palestinian complementizer, and bass takes the second clause. The two halves of the frame cannot be joined in the romanization.
ظ is written TH, the shadda doubles the ن and the first person past ending is a long ee. iftakart inno is just as common in Ramallah for a mistaken belief.
Long ii in yhiinak, with the verb starting on a cluster after la. A softener attached to a request, roughly if you would be so kind.
